input-validation: Input validation Input validation checks whether incoming data satisfies the structural and business constraints required at a system boundary before the system relies on it. Why a boundary needs a contract A browser, file, API client or hardware device can send unexpected data. A type annotation in application code does not prove that runtime input has that type. Validation makes assumptions explicit and rejects values the receiving operation cannot safely interpret. Client-side validation improves feedback. Server-side validation enforces the contract against clients that bypass the UI. Structure and meaning Syntactic validation checks representation: required fields, types, lengths and supported formats. Semantic validation checks meaning in context: an end date follows a start date, a requested quantity is within policy, or an inventory reference exists. A number can be syntactically valid while violating business rules. An identifier can be valid while referring to a record the caller is not allowed to access; that second question is authorization. A bounded TypeScript example This example enforces a small contract and fails closed. It does not implement persistence, access control or safe HTML rendering. The limits use JavaScript string length, which counts UTF-16 code units rather than user-perceived characters; choose the measurement appropriate to your actual requirement. Validation is one control among several Validation does not replace parameterized database queries, contextual output encoding, authentication, authorization or resource limits. A string can pass a title-length rule and still need safe handling when placed in HTML. Define normalization deliberately. Trimming a title may be acceptable; silently altering a password or opaque identifier can change its meaning. Validate after the interpretation step relevant to the contract and avoid ambiguous double decoding. Some systems must authenticate before costly parsing or perform several checks at different stages. This diagram shows responsibilities rather than one universally mandatory order. Failure handling and testing Return actionable errors without exposing internal stack traces or secrets. Bound request size before expensive parsing. Log enough context to diagnose repeated failures, but do not log credentials or full sensitive payloads. Test missing fields, wrong types, boundary lengths, extra properties and valid-but-unauthorized identifiers. Include valid input to show that the contract remains usable. Learning progression Start with serialization and API contracts. Then trace one value from an HTTP request to storage and display. authentication: Authentication Authentication establishes confidence in a claimed identity using credentials or other evidence; it does not itself decide which operations that identity may perform. Identity proof and session state A user may prove possession of a password, cryptographic authenticator or other credential. After successful authentication, a session or token allows subsequent requests to be associated with that identity. The application must still perform authorization for protected operations. Knowing who a user is does not grant access to every record. Example: signing in A server verifies credentials through an appropriate authentication mechanism, creates a session and sends the client a session reference. Later requests present that reference. Session expiration, revocation and account recovery are part of the design, not optional cleanup details. Do not store plaintext passwords or invent a custom password-storage algorithm. Use established authentication libraries and reviewed mechanisms. Failure and attack resistance Rate limits and monitoring can help detect guessing. Error messages should avoid unnecessary account enumeration. Recovery flows need the same care as sign-in because a weak recovery path can bypass strong primary authentication. Use HTTPS to protect credentials and session traffic in transit. Secure cookie settings and CSRF defenses depend on the selected session architecture. A session represents a user's authenticated state across multiple HTTP requests. HTTP is stateless: each request is independent. Sessions provide a way for a server to remember a user's authentication state. Example: 1. User logs in. 2. Server creates a session. 3. Server stores session data. 4. Server sends a session identifier to the browser. 5. Browser sends that identifier with subsequent requests. 6. Server looks up the session and identifies the user. Q13.25. Where can sessions be stored? Common options: - In-memory storage. - Redis. - Database. - Dedicated session store. For production applications with multiple backend instances, a shared store such as Redis is preferable to process-local memory. Imagine: If the session exists only in API 1's memory, a request routed to API 2 may not find it. A shared Redis session store solves this issue. Q13.26. JWT vs session: which should you use? Use sessions when: - Server-side revocation is important. - You want centralized session state. - Browser-based authentication is your primary use case. - You need convenient device/session management. Use JWT access tokens when: - Multiple APIs need to verify tokens. - You need portable signed claims. - Stateless access-token verification is useful. - You have a deliberate token expiration and revocation strategy. authorization: Authorization Authorization determines whether a subject may perform a requested action on a resource under the current policy and context. Subject, action and resource Authentication may identify a user. Authorization then asks whether that user can read a particular note, update an inventory record or administer settings. Policies can use roles, attributes, relationships and resource ownership. A role name alone is not a complete universal access model. A record-level example A signed-in user requests /notes/123 . The server must check whether note 123 belongs to the user or is shared with them. Hiding the link in the UI does not protect the route. A syntactically valid identifier is not evidence of access. Enforce checks at the server-side operation boundary and apply least privilege. Deny by default when policy is missing or uncertain. Common failures Checking only “is logged in,” trusting a client-supplied owner ID or protecting list pages but not direct record routes can expose data. Import/export and background-job paths also need policy enforcement. Caching a decision can become unsafe when ownership or permissions change; define invalidation and re-check critical operations. Practice Create an access matrix for owner, shared reader and unrelated user. Test read, edit, delete and export separately. Git is a distributed version-control system that records project snapshots and their history, supporting local work and collaboration through repositories and references. Working tree, index and history The working tree contains checked-out files. The index stages content for the next commit. A commit records a snapshot with parent history and metadata. Branches are movable references to commits, not separate physical folders by definition. GitHub is a hosting and collaboration service; it is not the Git version-control mechanism itself. testing: Software testing Choose the scope of a check !Testing scopes from unit through integration, API and browser, with production monitoring as feedback. A unit test isolates a small behavior; integration tests examine boundaries between components; API and browser tests exercise wider paths. These scopes overlap and need not run in a strict sequence. Production monitoring supplies feedback but does not replace pre-release tests. Use the test strategy article to decide which checks fit a particular risk. Software testing evaluates behavior using planned inputs, observations and expected outcomes to reveal defects and provide evidence about requirements. Different scopes answer different questions A unit test isolates a small behavior. An integration test checks cooperating components, such as an API and persistence. An end-to-end test exercises a user-visible workflow through a larger system. These labels vary across teams; state the actual boundary and dependencies of each test. Example: saving a note A meaningful test creates a note, reloads the application and checks that its content remains. A test that only checks the save function was called does not prove persistence. Failure cases include invalid input, missing permissions, unavailable storage and duplicate requests. Input validation and authorization each need different test cases. Limits and reliability Passing tests are evidence for the cases exercised, not proof of universal correctness. Brittle tests can fail after harmless presentation changes; excessive mocking can hide broken integration. Make test data deterministic and isolate it from real personal data. Needs review: examples and claims retain their source context; reading does not certify proficiency. Software Testing Fundamentals Q14.1. What is software testing? Software testing is the process of evaluating an application to identify defects and verify that it behaves according to its requirements. Imagine you build a student management application with these features: - Register students. - Log in. - View student profiles. - Update student details. - Delete student records. Testing checks whether these features work under expected and unexpected conditions. For example: | Input | Expected result | | ------------------------ | ----------------- | | Valid email and password | Login succeeds | | Incorrect password | Login rejected | | Empty email | Validation error | | Non-existent account | Appropriate error | | Expired JWT | Request rejected | Important: Testing can reveal the presence of defects, but it cannot prove that software is completely defect-free. Q14.2. Why is software testing important? 1. Detects bugs before production. 2. Helps prevent security vulnerabilities. 3. Verifies business requirements. 4. Reduces maintenance costs. 5. Prevents existing functionality from breaking. 6. Improves application reliability. 7. Builds confidence when developers modify code. Consider an insurance application. If the premium calculation is incorrect, a customer might be charged the wrong amount. Testing financial calculations therefore protects business operations, not just code quality. Q14.3. What is verification vs validation? | Verification | Validation | | -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | | Are we building the product correctly? | Are we building the correct product? | | Checks specifications and design | Checks actual application behaviour | | Can include reviews and inspections | Usually involves executing the software | | Focuses on conformance to requirements | Focuses on user needs | Example requirement: > A user must not be able to submit a registration form without an email address. - Verification: Review the design and implementation against the requirement. - Validation: Run the application, submit the form without an email, and check that it is rejected. Q14.4. Manual vs automation testing Manual testing: A tester executes test cases manually without writing automation scripts. Automation testing: Scripts and tools execute tests automatically and compare actual results with expected results. | Manual testing | Automation testing | | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | | Human executes test cases | Scripts execute test cases | | Useful for exploratory testing | Useful for repeatable tests | | Often slower for repetitive tasks | Efficient for repeated execution | | Less initial setup | Requires automation development | | Human observation is valuable | Consistent assertions and reports | Interview point: Automation does not replace manual testing. Exploratory testing, usability evaluation and situations requiring human judgment still benefit from manual testing. Testing Levels and Types Q14.5. Explain the four major testing levels Level 1 Unit testing Tests individual functions or components. Example: Verify that calculatePremium() returns the correct insurance premium. Level 2 Integration testing Tests interactions between components. Example: Verify that an Express API correctly saves a student record to PostgreSQL. Level 3 System testing Tests the complete integrated application. Example: Register, log in, submit an application and view its status. Level 4 Acceptance testing Checks whether the system meets business and user requirements. Example: A business stakeholder verifies that an insurance claim follows the required workflow. Q14.6. Functional vs non-functional testing Functional testing verifies what the application does. Examples: - Login works. - User can submit a form. - API returns the correct response. - Payment status updates correctly. Non-functional testing evaluates how well the application works. Examples: - Performance testing. - Load testing. - Stress testing. - Security testing. - Accessibility testing. - Compatibility testing. - Usability testing. An API might be functionally correct but take 15 seconds to respond. It passes a functional check but may fail performance expectations. Q14.7. Smoke, sanity and regression testing | Type | Meaning | Example | | ---------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | Smoke | Basic build verification | Can the application start? | | Sanity | Focused check after a small change | Does updated login validation work? | | Regression | Checks existing functionality after changes | Did the login change break registration? | Remember: - Smoke testing checks whether the build is stable enough for further testing. - Sanity testing checks a specific change or area. - Regression testing checks for unintended side effects. Q14.8. What is exploratory testing? Exploratory testing is an approach where testers simultaneously learn the application, design tests and execute them. While testing registration, you might try: - Submitting empty fields. - Pasting unusually long text. - Refreshing during submission. - Opening the same page in multiple tabs. - Clicking submit repeatedly. - Using unexpected characters. It is useful when requirements are incomplete or when testers want to discover unexpected behaviours. Q14.9. Positive vs negative testing Positive testing: Valid input should produce the expected result. Negative testing: Invalid input should be handled correctly. A good test suite includes both. debugging: Debugging Debugging is the evidence-driven process of locating, explaining and correcting the causes of unexpected system behavior. Reproduce, observe, explain Start with expected versus actual behavior, the environment and a minimal reproduction. Gather evidence, form a hypothesis, change one relevant variable and compare the result. A symptom disappearing after a restart does not establish its cause. Breakpoints and the call stack reveal execution state. Network traces reveal requests and timing. Hardware instruments reveal signals software logs may not capture. Example: missing sensor data Distinguish a sensor that never responds, a parser rejecting bytes, a queue dropping records and a UI failing to display them. Each hypothesis predicts different evidence. For a web page, a successful HTTP response does not prove that its contents were valid or rendered correctly. Reliable fixes Preserve the failing evidence, apply the smallest justified correction and verify the original case plus a nearby regression case. Record why the fix addresses the mechanism. Redact secrets from logs and screenshots. Avoid repeatedly modifying production data while guessing. Practice Create a troubleshooting record with reproduction steps, observations, hypotheses, rejected explanations and final validation. Assessment: another person should be able to follow the reasoning and reproduce the result. Continue with testing, observability and concurrency for timing-related failures. ci-cd: Continuous integration and delivery Continuous integration frequently integrates changes with automated checks; continuous delivery keeps changes releasable, while continuous deployment automatically releases eligible changes under defined policy. Pipeline responsibilities A typical pipeline checks out an exact revision, installs declared dependencies, runs selected tests and builds an artifact. A delivery stage promotes that artifact to an environment. Continuous delivery and continuous deployment are related practices with different release decisions. A green pipeline should have a clear meaning rather than imply that every possible risk was tested. Example A documentation platform can validate content IDs, test relationship navigation, type-check its code and build static assets on each proposed change. A deployment then uses the validated revision. Use Git history to connect a release with its source and checks. Security and failure handling Build scripts execute code. Limit credentials, review third-party actions and avoid exposing deployment secrets to untrusted contributions. Pin or constrain dependencies according to the project's update policy. Define what happens when deployment partially fails. Rollback may require handling database or content-format compatibility, not just replacing application files. Practice Write a pipeline diagram listing trigger, inputs, checks, artifact and release gate. Identify which failures stop delivery. Assessment: explain how to reproduce the build and how to trace a deployed artifact to a commit. Continue with testing and observability. observability: Observability Observability is the ability to investigate a system's internal behavior through the evidence it exposes, commonly including logs, metrics and traces. Evidence for questions Metrics summarize quantities over time. Logs record events and context. Traces connect operations across a request's path. Each reveals different aspects of a failure; collecting all three without a question can still leave a system difficult to understand. Monitoring checks known conditions. Observability also supports investigating failures that were not anticipated in advance. Example: slow article search Measure request latency and error rate. Correlate a slow request with a trace through content lookup and persistence. Inspect an associated event for a failed dependency, without logging the user's entire private query history. DNS, connection establishment, application work and database work can each contribute latency. Trade-offs and privacy High-cardinality labels can make metrics expensive. Detailed logs can contain personal data or secrets. Sampling and retention reduce cost but affect the evidence available during an incident. Define user-facing reliability goals before setting alert thresholds. An alert should guide a useful response instead of merely announcing activity. Practice Instrument one operation with duration, outcome and a correlation identifier. Trigger a controlled failure and reconstruct what happened. Assessment: distinguish absence of an error log from proof of successful service. Continue with debugging, testing and CI/CD. References and verification These sources are provided for claim review. machine-learning: Machine learning Machine learning develops models whose behavior is fitted from data rather than specified entirely as explicit rules. Learning a useful pattern is different from demonstrating that the pattern generalizes. The learning problem A supervised model learns from examples paired with target values. An unsupervised method looks for structure without that same target labeling. The task determines what data, objective, and evaluation are appropriate; “AI” is not a synonym for one particular algorithm. For a sensor-quality classifier, the input might contain recent measurements and device metadata. The target records a confirmed fault. A timestamp or maintenance flag written only after the fault can accidentally reveal the answer during training. Training and evaluation Define a simple baseline before fitting a more complicated model. Separate fitting data from evaluation data, and choose a split that reflects deployment: future observations or previously unseen devices may require time-based or grouped separation. Fit preprocessing on training data and apply the fitted transformation to held-out data. Fitting normalization or feature selection on the complete dataset can leak information into evaluation. See the scikit-learn pitfalls guide. Reliability and limitations An average score can hide poor results for uncommon cases. Record errors by meaningful groups, compare costs of false positives and false negatives, and document uncertain labels. A distribution change can invalidate a previously useful model. Treat sensitive training examples as protected data. Model output still needs checks appropriate to its downstream use. Practice and progression Build a small reproducible baseline, keep the held-out examples separate, and report both its metric and three failure cases. Assessment: explain why your evaluation estimates the intended deployment behavior. Data engineering supplies dependable inputs; testing checks the surrounding system; observability helps detect changes after deployment. Continue to embeddings and recommendation systems.
embeddings: Embeddings An embedding represents an item as a vector in a space intended to preserve useful relationships for a task. Items may be words, passages, images, products, users, or other structured inputs. Representation is a modeling choice The dimensions of a learned vector generally do not have simple human-readable meanings. Nearness means similarity under a particular representation and distance function, not guaranteed factual equivalence. In a two-tower retrieval model, one model encodes the query and another encodes candidates into compatible vector spaces. A scoring operation compares the two. This is illustrated in TensorFlow Recommenders. A small similarity example For nonzero vectors, cosine similarity divides the dot product by the product of their lengths. This JavaScript example uses tiny illustrative vectors, not outputs from a trained language model: Production code also needs finite-value checks and bounds on dimensions and resource use. Some retrieval models use dot product rather than cosine; use the scoring rule the model was designed for. Common failures Vectors from incompatible models or preprocessing pipelines should not be mixed in one index without a justified transformation. Record model identity, dimensionality, input preparation, and index version. Embedding a private document does not remove its sensitivity. Apply access controls to both stored content and retrieval results. Approximate nearest-neighbor search trades exactness for efficiency and needs measurement. Exercise Write ten domain questions and manually label relevant documents. Compare retrieval results with those labels, including similar-looking but irrelevant passages. Assessment: distinguish retrieval quality from the quality of a generated answer. Continue with RAG, machine learning, and data engineering.
rag: Retrieval-augmented generation Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with a generative model. A system retrieves material relevant to an input and makes that material available during answer generation. Why retrieve before generating? A model's parameters are not a complete, current, auditable copy of your documents. Retrieval creates a path to source material that can be maintained separately. It does not guarantee that the model understands or faithfully uses that material. The original RAG paper studied a particular combination of a sequence-to-sequence generator and dense retrieval over Wikipedia. Contemporary engineering usage is broader; an arbitrary document chatbot does not necessarily implement the paper's training method. Architecture and boundaries Data engineering manages ingestion, updates, deletion, and reproducibility. Embeddings can support semantic retrieval, but keyword search or hybrid retrieval can also be suitable. A vector database is an implementation choice, not the definition of RAG. Example: asking the codex a question Suppose the question is “Does a USB connector prove that a board supports HID?” A retrieval stage should find the exact board documentation and the USB HID explanation. An answer should distinguish a physical connector, controller capabilities, and firmware support. If no exact model is known, the system should ask for that information or state the limitation. A source about one board variant is not evidence for every variant. Evaluate the stages separately Start with a fixed set of questions and expected supporting passages. Measure whether retrieval finds those passages before adding a generator. Then review answer correctness, source support, citation accuracy, and behavior when the corpus lacks an answer. Removing a document must remove its retrievable chunks as well. Track document versions and source ranges so an answer can be traced to the evidence actually used. Security and reliability Retrieved text is untrusted input. It must not override application instructions or grant permissions. Filter access before material is exposed to a model or user, and recheck policy where appropriate. Authorization applies to individual documents and derived data. Long context, stale indexes, poorly chosen chunks, and superficially similar passages can produce confident mistakes. Do not treat a displayed citation as proof that it supports the accompanying claim. Practical exercise Build a retrieval-only prototype over ten public technical documents. Save query, retrieved source IDs, source versions, and human relevance judgments. Add generation only after this baseline is understandable. Assessment: demonstrate an answerable question, an unsupported question, a stale document, and a denied document without exposing restricted content. Continue with testing, observability, and input validation.
data-engineering: Data engineering Data engineering designs and operates systems that collect, transform, store, and deliver data for dependable use. Its output is a usable data product with understood meaning, quality, ownership, and operational limits. From events to useful records A sensor reading is not useful merely because a number arrived. Consumers need its unit, timestamp convention, device identity, validity, and handling of missing or duplicate values. A schema documents structure; a data contract also explains meaning and expectations. Batch pipelines process bounded collections on a schedule or trigger. Streaming pipelines process ongoing arrivals, but still require explicit choices about ordering, late events, retries, and state. Example: a laboratory dataset Keep the original sensor events, record the schema version, and derive a table of daily measurements. When an event is repeated after a retry, use a suitable stable event identifier to avoid unintended duplication. When units change, make that transformation explicit rather than silently mixing values. ETL describes one ordering of extraction, transformation, and loading. Serialization defines the representations that ingestion and storage exchange. Quality and operations Check completeness, freshness, uniqueness, and plausible ranges according to the actual use case. A successful job exit does not establish that the delivered data is correct. Record lineage so an unexpected result can be traced to input versions and transformations. Restrict access to sensitive fields and define retention and deletion behavior across derived copies. Test replay, partial failure, and schema changes on controlled data before production use. Practice Create a small pipeline that loads timestamped observations, quarantines malformed records, and produces a summary. Run it twice against the same source and explain its duplicate behavior. Assessment: reproduce an output row from its inputs and show a freshness failure. Related skills include input validation, testing, observability, and machine learning.
etl: Extract, transform, load ETL is a data integration pattern in which data is extracted from sources, transformed into a usable representation, and loaded into a destination. ELT changes the order by loading before performing selected transformations in the destination system. Responsibilities at each stage Extraction defines what is read and how progress is tracked. Transformation defines mapping, cleaning, normalization, and derived values. Loading defines how destination records are inserted, replaced, or merged. Neither acronym specifies a universal tool, schedule, or consistency guarantee. Data engineering supplies the broader operational design. A measurement example A source contains a device ID, an event timestamp, a temperature, and its unit. Extract the original rows, validate the contract, convert supported units into the documented target unit, and load the result with the original event ID. Do not convert missing readings to zero. Quarantine unknown units with an explanation. Keep the source representation so an incorrect transformation can be repaired and replayed. Failure and recovery An interruption can occur after some rows are written but before the job records success. Design retry behavior deliberately: stable keys, transactional boundaries, checkpoints, or staging tables may be appropriate. A checkpoint is only useful when its relationship to committed output is understood. Source changes during extraction can create an inconsistent view. Decide whether a snapshot, change log, watermark, or other mechanism meets the use case rather than assuming one read sees everything at one instant. Exercise Import a small CSV-like source into a test table. Include a duplicate event, a bad timestamp, and an unsupported unit. Rerun after a simulated interruption and reconcile source, accepted, rejected, and destination counts. Assessment: explain every missing or repeated row. Continue with serialization, input validation, and testing.
serialization: Serialization and file formats Serialization maps structured values into a representation that can be stored or transmitted. Deserialization interprets that representation to recover values according to a format and schema. Extension, format, and encoding A filename extension is a naming convention. A .dat file may contain text, packed binary records, or an application-specific format; the extension does not establish its layout. Renaming a file does not convert its contents. Text encoding maps characters to bytes. A format describes how values are organized. A schema adds constraints and meaning, such as which fields are required and which unit a number represents. A small JSON example Successful parsing does not validate an application contract. Check required fields, supported units, numeric limits, and resource bounds before using the result. JSON does not preserve arbitrary language-specific objects, functions, or object identity. Binary formats A fixed-width binary record requires agreement on field sizes, byte order, signedness, and alignment. Changing one of those assumptions can produce plausible but incorrect numbers. Preserve a format version and test against known byte sequences. Serialization is different from compression and encryption. A binary representation is not automatically secret. Some deserialization mechanisms can construct executable objects; choose a format and parser suitable for untrusted input. Exercise Document a sensor-message schema and round-trip several valid examples. Reject malformed text, missing fields, and oversized input. Assessment: explain what parsing guarantees and what input validation must still check. Connect this to UART, MQTT, and ETL.
recommendation-systems: Recommendation systems A recommendation system selects and orders items for a user or context using an explicit objective and available evidence. Its behavior depends on data, candidate selection, scoring, constraints, and feedback. Retrieval and ranking Candidate retrieval narrows a large collection to a tractable set. Ranking then scores or orders those candidates for the current request. A further stage can apply eligibility, diversity, or product constraints. This division is illustrated by the TensorFlow retrieval tutorial. Content-based approaches use item characteristics. Collaborative approaches learn from patterns across interactions. Embeddings can represent users or items for similarity-based retrieval, but a system need not use a neural model to recommend useful material. Example: next topics in the codex A transparent baseline recommends documented prerequisites that a learner has not completed. It can then suggest a connected concept relevant to a chosen engineering role. This uses the knowledge graph and explicit learning state rather than inferring ability from clicks alone. Compare that baseline with a learned ranker only when there is enough appropriate data and a meaningful evaluation objective. Feedback is imperfect evidence A click can mean curiosity, confusion, or accidental selection. More engagement does not necessarily mean more learning or satisfaction. Exposure also affects which feedback is observed: unseen items cannot receive the same interaction opportunities. Avoid treating a vendor's illustrative system description as disclosure of its complete current implementation. Research claims about social-media behavior and legal disputes remain in the original archive pending separate verification. Practice Build a small recommendation list with an explanation for every item. Compare relevance, coverage, and duplicate content against a simple chronological baseline. Assessment: describe cold-start behavior and one feedback loop that could narrow recommendations. Related concepts include machine learning, data engineering, and testing.

Answer: CSS comments are written using / and / . Example: Comments are ignored by the browser when applying styles. Q1.70. What are CSS selectors? Answer: CSS selectors identify the HTML elements to which we want to apply styles. Q1.71. What is CSS specificity? Answer: CSS specificity determines which CSS rule is applied when multiple rules target the same element. The general priority is: 1. Inline styles. 2. ID selectors. 3. Class, attribute and pseudo-class selectors. 4. Element and pseudo-element selectors. The !important declaration can override normal cascade priorities, but it should be used carefully. Q1.72. What is CSS inheritance? Answer: CSS inheritance means some CSS properties are automatically passed from a parent element to its child elements. For example, if I set color: blue on a parent container, its child text elements usually inherit that color. Properties such as color and font-family are commonly inherited, while margin and padding are not inherited by default. Q1.73. What are CSS combinators? Answer: CSS combinators describe relationships between elements and help us select elements based on their position in the HTML structure. Common combinators are: - Descendant ( A B ): Selects all matching descendants. - Child ( A > B ): Selects direct children. - Adjacent sibling ( A + B ): Selects the immediately following sibling. - General sibling ( A ~ B ): Selects subsequent matching siblings. Q1.74. What are pseudo-classes in CSS? Answer: Pseudo-classes select elements based on their state or position. Examples: - :hover selects an element when the pointer is over it. - :focus selects an element when it receives focus. - :first-child selects the first child. - :checked selects checked form controls. For example, button:hover changes a button's appearance when the user hovers over it. Q1.75. What are pseudo-elements in CSS? Answer: Pseudo-elements allow us to style a specific part of an element or insert generated content. Common examples include: - ::before - ::after - ::first-letter - ::first-line - ::placeholder For example, p::first-letter can style the first letter of every paragraph. Q1.76. What is the CSS box model? Answer: The CSS box model explains how the browser calculates the space occupied by an HTML element. It contains four parts: 1. Content: The actual text or image. 2. Padding: Space between content and border. 3. Border: The boundary around the element. 4. Margin: Space outside the border. For example, if a card has padding of 20px, its content gets 20px of internal spacing from the border. Q1.77. What is the difference between margin and padding? Answer: - Margin: Creates space outside an element's border. - Padding: Creates space between the content and its border. For example, margin separates two cards, while padding creates space inside a card around its text. Q1.78. What is the box-sizing property in CSS? Answer: The box-sizing property determines how the browser calculates an element's total width and height. There are two common values: - content-box : Width and height apply only to the content. - border-box : Width and height include content, padding and border. Example: Using border-box makes layout calculations easier because padding and borders are included in the declared dimensions. Q1.79. What are the different CSS display properties? Answer: The display property controls how an element participates in the layout. Common values include: - block : Starts on a new line and normally takes available width. - inline : Stays within the current line. - inline-block : Stays inline but supports width and height. - flex : Creates a flex container. - grid : Creates a grid container. - none : Removes the element from the layout. Q1.80. What does display: inline-block do? Answer: inline-block allows an element to remain within the current line while still supporting width, height, margin and padding in a more predictable way than a normal inline element. It is useful when we want multiple small elements to appear next to each other while controlling their dimensions. Q1.81. What is CSS Flexbox? Answer: Flexbox is a CSS layout system designed to arrange elements along one main axis, either horizontally or vertically. It makes alignment, spacing and distribution of elements easier. For example, I can use Flexbox to center a login form or arrange navigation links in a horizontal row. Q1.82. What is CSS Grid? Answer: CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system that allows us to arrange elements using rows and columns. It is useful for complex layouts such as dashboards, galleries and webpage sections. For example, I can use Grid to create a dashboard with a sidebar, header and multiple content cards. Q1.83. What is the difference between Flexbox and Grid? Answer: | Flexbox | Grid | | -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | | Primarily one-dimensional | Two-dimensional | | Works along a row or column | Works with rows and columns together | | Useful for navigation bars and component alignment | Useful for complete page layouts and dashboards | | Content often determines the layout | Layout can be defined using explicit tracks | Both can be used together in the same application. Q1.84. What is CSS positioning? Answer: The position property controls how an element is positioned within a webpage. Its main values are: - static : Default positioning. - relative : Positioned relative to its normal position. - absolute : Positioned relative to its nearest positioned ancestor. - fixed : Positioned relative to the viewport. - sticky : Behaves normally until a scroll threshold is reached, then sticks. The z-index property controls stacking order when the elements participate in compatible stacking contexts. For example, we can position a notification badge over the corner of a profile image. Q1.86. What is CSS overflow? Answer: The overflow property controls what happens when content is larger than its container. Common values are: - visible : Content can extend outside the container. - hidden : Extra content is clipped. - scroll : Displays scrolling controls. - auto : Adds scrolling when required. For example, a chat panel can use overflow-y: auto to allow vertical scrolling through messages. Q1.87. What is the CSS float property? Answer: The float property moves an element towards the left or right side of its container, allowing surrounding text to flow around it. It was commonly used for layouts in older websites but is now mainly useful for text wrapping around images. Modern layouts generally use Flexbox or Grid. Q1.88. How can you vertically center text or an element using CSS? Answer: One of the simplest methods is to use Flexbox. Here, justify-content aligns content along the main axis, while align-items aligns it along the cross axis. Q1.89. How can you center an image using CSS? Answer: We can use Flexbox to center an image horizontally and vertically. We can also use margin: auto for horizontal centering when the image or element has an appropriate block layout and width. Q1.90. What is responsive web design? Answer: Responsive web design means creating websites that automatically adjust their layout and appearance according to the user's screen size and device. Answer: We can make websites responsive using media queries, flexible layouts and relative units. Example: This changes a two-column layout into a single-column layout on smaller screens. Q1.92. What are media queries in CSS? Answer: Media queries allow us to apply CSS rules based on conditions such as screen width, orientation and device characteristics. Example: This hides the sidebar when the viewport width is 768px or smaller. Q1.93. What does the float property do, and how is it different from Flexbox? Answer: Float moves an element to the left or right and allows text to wrap around it. Flexbox creates a flexible layout that controls the alignment and distribution of child elements. Float is mainly useful for wrapping text around images, while Flexbox is better for modern component layouts. Q1.94. What does the alpha value in RGBA represent? Answer: RGBA stands for Red, Green, Blue and Alpha. The alpha value controls the transparency of a color. - 0 : Fully transparent. - 0.5 : 50% opacity. - 1 : Fully opaque. Example: This creates a semi-transparent red background. Q1.95. What are HSL colors in CSS? Answer: HSL stands for Hue, Saturation and Lightness. - Hue: Represents the color, usually from 0° to 360°. - Saturation: Controls color intensity. - Lightness: Controls brightness. Example: HSL is useful because it makes adjusting color shades more intuitive. Q1.96. What are CSS border properties? Answer: CSS border properties control the appearance of an element's border. The main properties are: - border-width : Controls thickness. - border-style : Controls appearance, such as solid, dashed or dotted. - border-color : Controls the border color. - border-radius : Creates rounded corners. Example: Q1.97. What are CSS transitions? Answer: CSS transitions allow property changes to happen smoothly over a specified duration. For example: The background color changes smoothly when the user hovers over the button. Q1.98. What are CSS animations? Answer: CSS animations allow elements to change their styles over time without requiring JavaScript. They are generally created using @keyframes and the animation property. They are useful for loading indicators, moving elements and visual effects. Q1.99. What are CSS gradients? Answer: CSS gradients create smooth transitions between two or more colors without requiring image files. Common types are: - Linear gradient. - Radial gradient. - Conic gradient. Example: Q1.100. What are 2D and 3D transformations in CSS? Answer: CSS transformations allow us to rotate, scale, move or skew elements. - 2D transformations work along the X and Y axes. - 3D transformations also support depth along the Z axis. Needs review: examples and claims retain their source context; reading does not certify proficiency. Browser Rendering and DOM Q1.102. What is the DOM? Answer: DOM stands for Document Object Model. It is a programming interface that represents an HTML document as a tree of objects. JavaScript can use the DOM to access, modify, create and remove HTML elements dynamically. For example, when a user clicks an Add Task button, JavaScript can create a new task element and display it without reloading the page. Q1.103. What is the difference between HTML and DOM? Answer: - HTML is the markup language used to define the structure of a webpage. - DOM is the object-based representation of that document created by the browser. HTML defines the initial page structure, while JavaScript can modify the DOM dynamically without changing the original HTML source file. Q1.104. How does a browser render a webpage? Answer: The browser follows several steps to convert HTML, CSS and other resources into visible pixels. 1. Parses HTML and builds the DOM tree. 2. Parses CSS and builds the CSSOM tree. 3. Combines them to create the render tree. 4. Performs layout calculations. 5. Paints elements. 6. Composites the layers and displays the result. JavaScript can modify the DOM and CSSOM, which may cause parts of the rendering process to run again. Q1.105. What is the difference between DOM and CSSOM? Answer: - DOM: Represents the structure and content of an HTML document. - CSSOM: Represents the CSS rules and styles associated with the document. The browser combines the information from both to determine how visible elements should be rendered. Q1.106. What is the difference between reflow and repaint? Answer: - Reflow: Happens when the browser recalculates the layout or geometry of elements. - Repaint: Happens when the browser redraws the appearance of elements without necessarily recalculating their layout. For example, changing an element's width may cause reflow, while changing its background color generally causes repaint. Frequent layout changes can reduce performance, so we should avoid unnecessary DOM updates. Q1.107. How do you select HTML elements using JavaScript? Answer: JavaScript provides several DOM selection methods. Common methods include: querySelector() returns the first matching element, while querySelectorAll() returns a static NodeList containing all matching elements. Q1.108. How do you create and modify DOM elements using JavaScript? Answer: JavaScript provides DOM methods to create elements, update their content and attributes, and insert them into the document. Example: This creates a heading and adds it to the webpage. Q1.109. What is the difference between innerHTML and textContent ? Answer: - innerHTML gets or sets the HTML markup inside an element. - textContent gets or sets the text content without interpreting it as HTML. For example, assigning Hello to innerHTML creates bold text, while assigning it to textContent displays the characters as text. Interview point: Avoid inserting untrusted user input through innerHTML because it can create cross-site scripting vulnerabilities. Q1.110. What is getComputedStyle() ? Answer: getComputedStyle() is a browser API that returns the final computed CSS styles of an element after applying stylesheets, inheritance and the CSS cascade. Example: It is useful when we need to inspect the actual styles applied by the browser. Q1.111. What is getBoundingClientRect() ? Answer: getBoundingClientRect() returns the size and position of an element relative to the browser's viewport. It provides properties such as top , left , right , bottom , width and height . It is useful for positioning tooltips, overlays and inspection panels. Q1.112. What is MutationObserver? Answer: MutationObserver is a browser API that allows JavaScript to observe changes in the DOM. It can detect changes such as added elements, removed elements and modified attributes. For example, in a DOM inspection tool, MutationObserver can detect when a webpage dynamically adds new components. Q1.113. What is Shadow DOM? Answer: Shadow DOM is a browser feature that allows us to create an encapsulated DOM subtree inside a host element. It helps isolate the internal HTML and CSS of a component from the surrounding webpage. For example, a Chrome extension can use Shadow DOM for its floating inspection panel so that the website's CSS does not easily interfere with the extension's styles. Interview point: Shadow DOM provides encapsulation, not a complete security boundary. Q1.114. What are Web Components? Answer: Web Components are a collection of browser technologies that allow developers to create reusable custom HTML elements. Their main technologies include: - Custom Elements. - Shadow DOM. - HTML Templates. For example, we can create a reusable element that displays user information. Needs review: examples and claims retain their source context; reading does not certify proficiency. Browser Storage Q1.115. What is browser storage? Answer: Browser storage refers to the mechanisms that allow web applications to store data on the user's device. Common browser storage mechanisms include: - Cookies. - Local Storage. - Session Storage. - IndexedDB. For example, a task management application can use Local Storage to remember tasks after the user refreshes the page. Q1.116. What is Local Storage? Answer: Local Storage is a browser storage mechanism that stores key-value pairs as strings and keeps the data even after the browser is closed and reopened. It does not automatically expire. Example: It is useful for storing non-sensitive preferences and simple application data. Q1.117. What is Session Storage? Answer: Session Storage stores key-value pairs for a particular browser tab's session. The data normally remains available when the page is refreshed but is cleared when that tab's page session ends. For example, we can temporarily store information about a multi-step form. Q1.118. What are cookies? Answer: Cookies are small pieces of data stored by the browser and associated with a website. They are commonly used for session management, authentication and user preferences. Unlike Local Storage, cookies can be automatically included in matching HTTP requests. Q1.119. What is the difference between Local Storage, Session Storage and Cookies? Answer: | Feature | Local Storage | Session Storage | Cookies | | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------ | | Lifetime | Until removed | Usually until tab session ends | Depends on expiration settings | | Capacity | Usually around 5 MB or more, depending on browser | Usually around 5 MB | Usually around 4 KB per cookie | | Sent automatically with HTTP requests | No | No | Yes, when applicable | | Scope | Origin | Origin and tab session | Depends on domain and path | | Common use | Preferences | Temporary form data | Sessions and authentication | Interview point: Sensitive authentication cookies should generally use HttpOnly , Secure and appropriate SameSite settings. Q1.120. How do you create, read and delete cookies using JavaScript? Answer: JavaScript provides the document.cookie property to work with cookies that are accessible to JavaScript. Answer: IndexedDB is a browser database that allows applications to store larger amounts of structured data locally. Answer: - Local Storage: Simple synchronous key-value storage that stores strings. - IndexedDB: Asynchronous browser database that supports structured data, indexes and larger datasets. Local Storage is suitable for simple preferences, while IndexedDB is more suitable for complex offline application data. Interview question: What is Manifest V3, and why did you use it? Interview-ready answer Manifest V3 is the modern Chrome Extension platform architecture. Permissions control what an extension can access. Requesting unnecessary permissions can create security and privacy concerns. What are content scripts? Interview question: What is a content script? Interview-ready answer A content script is JavaScript that runs in the context of a webpage and can interact with its DOM. Chrome uses an isolated world for content scripts. The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) In traditional GIL-enabled CPython builds, the Global Interpreter Lock allows only one thread at a time to execute Python bytecode within a given interpreter. Important distinctions: - Threads can be useful for I/O-bound tasks. - Multiprocessing can use multiple processes for CPU-bound work. - Asynchronous programming is useful for coordinating many I/O operations. - Modern Python also has optional free-threaded CPython builds, so avoid saying that every Python implementation or build always has a GIL. Needs review: examples and claims retain their source context; reading does not certify proficiency. Database Normalization Normalization organizes relational data to reduce duplication and prevent data anomalies. Q8.12. What is normalization? It is the process of structuring database tables according to rules called normal forms. Consider a poorly designed table: | student id | student name | company name | drive role | | ---------- | ------------ | ------------ | ---------- | | 1 | Chirag | Google | SDE | | 1 | Chirag | Microsoft | QA | | 2 | Rahul | Google | SDE | Student and company information is repeated. This can cause: - Update anomaly: Changing a student's name requires updating multiple records. - Insertion anomaly: You cannot store a company until a drive or related record exists. - Deletion anomaly: Deleting the last drive record could accidentally remove the only stored company information. We separate the data into related tables. First Normal Form (1NF) - Each column contains atomic values. - No repeating groups or arrays of values in a single cell. - Each row is identifiable. Instead of storing Python, Java, SQL in one skills cell, use a separate student skills table with one skill per row. Second Normal Form (2NF) - Must satisfy 1NF. - Every non-key attribute must depend on the entire candidate key, not just part of a composite candidate key. For example, in a table keyed by (student id, drive id) , student name depends only on student id , not on the full key. It belongs in the students table. Third Normal Form (3NF) - Must satisfy 2NF. - Non-key attributes must not depend transitively on a candidate key. Example: If department name is stored in the student table, it depends on department id , not directly on the student's key. Separate departments into their own table. Q8.13. What is denormalization? Denormalization intentionally introduces redundancy to improve read performance or simplify certain access patterns. Example: Store a precomputed application count on a drive rather than calculating it every time. Trade-off: - Faster or simpler reads in certain workloads. - More complex writes and risk of inconsistent duplicated values. Interview answer: Normalize first to protect data integrity. Denormalize only when there is a demonstrated performance or reporting need and a strategy to keep duplicated data consistent. Needs review: examples and claims retain their source context; reading does not certify proficiency. Transactions, ACID and Concurrency What is a transaction? A transaction is a logical unit of database work. It allows multiple operations to succeed or fail together. Imagine a student accepts a company offer. The application must: 1. Update the offer status. 2. Update the application status. 3. Record the acceptance in the audit history. If the first two succeed but the audit record fails, the database may become inconsistent. A transaction ensures the operations are committed together or rolled back together. ACID properties - A — Atomicity: All operations succeed, or none are committed. - C — Consistency: A transaction preserves defined database constraints and integrity rules. - I — Isolation: Concurrent transactions are controlled so they do not produce unacceptable interference. - D — Durability: Once committed, changes survive failures according to the database's durability guarantees. Q8.18. Explain ACID with a practical example. When a student accepts an offer, the application status, offer status, and audit record should be updated as one transaction. Atomicity prevents partial completion; consistency preserves constraints; isolation controls concurrent updates; durability ensures the committed result is retained. SQL transaction example If something fails before the transaction commits: - COMMIT : Commits the transaction's changes. - ROLLBACK : Discards uncommitted changes. Transaction isolation levels | Isolation level | Key behaviour | | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Read Uncommitted | PostgreSQL treats it as Read Committed | | Read Committed | Each statement sees a committed snapshot | | Repeatable Read | Transaction sees a stable snapshot | | Serializable | Enforces behaviour equivalent to serial execution, potentially requiring retries | Q8.19. What are dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantom reads? - Dirty read: Reading uncommitted data from another transaction. PostgreSQL prevents this. - Non-repeatable read: Reading the same row twice and seeing different committed values. - Phantom read: Repeating a query and seeing a different set of rows due to changes by another transaction. PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read provides snapshot isolation and prevents non-repeatable reads and phantom reads in PostgreSQL, although serialization anomalies can still occur. Serializable provides stronger guarantees. Race conditions A race condition occurs when the result depends on the timing or ordering of concurrent operations. Example: Only one seat is available in a placement drive, and two students attempt to claim it simultaneously. A naive read-then-decrement approach can allow both to believe they obtained the last seat. One solution is an atomic conditional update: If no row is returned, no seat was available to claim. Q8.20. Optimistic vs pessimistic locking? - Pessimistic locking: Lock a record so competing transactions must wait or fail to acquire the lock. - Optimistic locking: Let operations proceed, but check a version or equivalent condition before accepting an update. Example: If zero rows are affected, another transaction changed the record first. The application should reload and retry or report a conflict. Q8.21. What is a lost update? Two transactions read the same original value and then overwrite each other's updates. Example: - Original stock = 10. - A reads 10 and calculates 9. - B reads 10 and calculates 8. - A writes 9. - B writes 8. The final value becomes 8 instead of 7. A database-level atomic update can prevent this specific pattern: Q8.22. What is row-level locking? Row-level locking locks selected rows to coordinate conflicting updates. PostgreSQL example: Another transaction trying to update or acquire a conflicting lock on that row may need to wait. Connected study Continue with software engineering and the complete study library.

Needs review: examples and claims retain their source context; reading does not certify proficiency. PostgreSQL Architecture Q8.23. What is PostgreSQL? PostgreSQL is an open-source object-relational database management system (ORDBMS). It supports: - Relational tables and SQL. - Transactions and ACID properties. - Constraints and indexes. - JSON and JSONB. - Views and materialized views. - Stored functions and triggers. - Extensions such as PostGIS. How PostgreSQL processes a query 1. Client sends SQL to PostgreSQL. 2. PostgreSQL parses and validates the query. 3. The planner/optimizer chooses a query plan. 4. The executor runs the plan. 5. Data is accessed through memory and storage structures. 6. Results are returned to the client. Shared buffers Shared buffers are PostgreSQL's main shared memory area for caching database pages. When a query needs a page, PostgreSQL can use a cached copy or read it from storage. WAL WAL stands for Write-Ahead Logging. PostgreSQL records changes in its write-ahead log before the corresponding data pages need to be written to their final locations. Why? - Crash recovery. - Durability. - Replication support. - Point-in-time recovery when combined with appropriate backups and archived WAL. Q8.24. What happens when a PostgreSQL transaction commits? In simplified terms: 1. The transaction's changes generate WAL records. 2. PostgreSQL ensures the relevant WAL is flushed according to configured durability settings. 3. The commit is acknowledged. 4. Changed data pages can be written later. 5. If a crash occurs, WAL supports recovery. A commit does not mean every modified data page is immediately written to the table file. MVCC MVCC stands for Multi-Version Concurrency Control. PostgreSQL uses row versions to allow readers and writers to work concurrently in many situations without readers blocking writers or writers blocking readers. An UPDATE typically creates a new row version rather than overwriting the old version in place. Old versions are later cleaned up through vacuuming when they are no longer needed. Q8.25. What is VACUUM? VACUUM helps reclaim space occupied by obsolete row versions for reuse and maintains visibility information. PostgreSQL's autovacuum normally performs maintenance automatically. ANALYZE updates statistics used by the query planner. Connected study Continue with software engineering and the complete study library.

A database connection is a communication session between an application and a database server. Creating and destroying connections for every request is inefficient. Q8.27. What is connection pooling? Connection pooling maintains a reusable collection of database connections. Typical flow: 1. An API request asks for a connection. 2. The pool provides an available connection. 3. The query runs. 4. Benefits: - Lower connection setup overhead. - Controlled database connection count. - Better resource utilization. - Improved application scalability. Q8.28. What happens when the pool is exhausted? SQL/relational databases store data in structured tables with defined schemas and relationships. Examples include PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Oracle. NoSQL databases use models such as documents, key-value pairs, graphs, or wide-column records. Examples include MongoDB, Redis, and Cassandra. | Feature | SQL | NoSQL | | -------------- | ----------------------- | ---------------------------- | | Data model | Usually tables | Documents, key-value, etc. | | Schema | Generally predefined | Often flexible | | Relationships | Foreign keys and joins | Often embedded or referenced | | Query language | SQL | Varies | | Transactions | Commonly strong support | Depends on database | When would you choose PostgreSQL over MongoDB? Choose PostgreSQL when an application has structured data, strong relationships, transactional workflows, and consistency requirements. A recruitment platform has relationships between students, drives, and applications, making PostgreSQL a natural choice. MongoDB may suit document-oriented data with varying structures or nested documents. NoSQL does not automatically mean faster or more scalable; the decision depends on workload and access patterns. Q9.2. What is NoSQL? NoSQL means “Not Only SQL.” It refers to database systems that use data models other than, or in addition to, traditional relational tables. The four main categories are: | Category | How it stores data | Examples | | ----------- | ---------------------------------- | --------------------- | | Document | JSON-like documents | MongoDB, Couchbase | | Key-value | Values associated with unique keys | Redis, DynamoDB | | Wide-column | Rows and flexible column families | Cassandra, HBase | | Graph | Nodes and relationships | Neo4j, Amazon Neptune | Q9.3. Q9.17. What is an embedded document? An embedded document stores related information inside the same parent document. Advantages - Related data can be retrieved in one query. - Natural representation of nested structures. - Atomic updates to a single document. - Fewer cross-collection queries. Disadvantages - Documents can become large. - Data duplication can occur. - Updating duplicated data becomes harder. - Arrays that grow indefinitely can cause design problems. Q9.18. What is a reference in MongoDB? A reference stores the id of another document. students collection: applications collection: The application document points to a student and a drive without embedding their entire records. Advantages of references - Avoids excessive duplication. - Related records can be managed independently. - Suitable for many-to-many relationships. - Better when related data is large or independently updated. Disadvantages - May require additional queries or aggregation. - MongoDB does not automatically enforce ordinary references as foreign keys. - Application code must manage referential integrity. Needs review: examples and claims retain their source context; reading does not certify proficiency. Virtual DOM and Reconciliation Q10.17. What is the Virtual DOM? Answer: The Virtual DOM is a common informal name for the in-memory representation of the UI that React works with. React elements describe what the UI should look like. When state or props change, React calculates the next UI representation and reconciles it with the previous one. It then commits the necessary changes to the actual DOM. Simplified flow: 1. Component renders. 2. React receives the new element description. 3. React reconciles it with the previous description. 4. React determines necessary updates. 5. React commits relevant changes to the DOM. Important: React does not necessarily recreate the entire real DOM every time a component renders. Q10.18. What is React reconciliation? Answer: Reconciliation is React's process for comparing the previous rendered element tree with the new one to determine how the UI should be updated. React uses element types, positions and keys to determine whether to preserve or replace component state and DOM. For example: If the component type changes from Login to Dashboard , React treats them as different component identities. Q10.19. What are React keys, and why are they important? Answer: Keys help React identify individual elements in a list across renders. Incorrect: Correct: Why keys matter: - Identify elements between renders. - Help preserve component identity. - Help React correctly insert, remove and reorder elements. - Avoid incorrect state association in lists. Why avoid array indexes as keys? Consider: If Amit is deleted, the indexes shift. React may associate previous component state with the wrong student. Prefer stable IDs. Use an index only when the list is static and will not be reordered, inserted into or deleted from. Q10.20. Does React update the entire page whenever state changes? Answer: No. A state update schedules React to render the component again. React reconciles the new output and commits the required changes. A render does not automatically mean the entire DOM is replaced. Also remember: - A component may render without its DOM output changing. - A parent rendering may cause its children to render. - Memoization can sometimes skip child rendering. - Reconciliation and DOM commit are separate steps. This is an illustrative formula; actual implementations may include a maximum delay and random jitter. What is jitter? Jitter adds randomness to retry delays. It prevents many clients from retrying at exactly the same time. What is a circuit breaker pattern? Interview question: Explain circuit breaker in your project. Interview-ready answer The circuit breaker pattern is a reliability technique that temporarily stops requests to an unhealthy service to avoid repeatedly calling a provider that is failing. DOMLens implements a cascading fallback approach across configured AI models. It can move away from models experiencing capacity errors or unavailable model IDs. For example, it handles: - HTTP 503 capacity failures using retry and fallback logic. - HTTP 404 model-not-found errors by removing or skipping the unavailable model. Three common circuit breaker states Closed Requests are allowed normally. Open Requests are blocked temporarily because of failures. Half-open A limited request tests whether the service has recovered. These are the standard circuit-breaker states. FastAPI is a Python web framework for HTTP APIs. A path operation maps a method and URL to a Python function. Type annotations and Pydantic models describe request data; the framework uses those declarations for validation and API documentation. An ASGI server such as Uvicorn runs the application. Follow the request through routing, parameter parsing, dependencies, endpoint logic and response serialization. Framework validation does not replace business rules, database constraints or authorization. Request Models, Response Models and Errors Use separate input and output models when the fields differ. For example, a registration request may contain a password, but the response must not include it or its stored hash. A response model validates and filters returned data to the declared output shape. Official response-model guide. This is an in-memory teaching example; it loses data on restart and is unsuitable as shared storage across multiple server workers. The model checks length; the endpoint also rejects a whitespace-only name. A missing student produces 404 rather than an unhandled lookup error. A production implementation delegates persistence to the database phase's transaction and uniqueness rules. Dependencies, Routers and Resource Lifetime A dependency supplies a reusable requirement such as validated pagination, a database session or the current user. FastAPI resolves declared dependencies before running the endpoint. A dependency using yield can arrange resource cleanup. Official dependency guide. Use APIRouter to group endpoints by feature. Keep routing, business decisions and persistence separable so business behavior can be tested without a live HTTP request. Reuse an engine/pool, but give each request an appropriate session lifetime; do not share one mutable session among concurrent requests. When Should an Endpoint Use async def? Use async def when calling awaitable I/O libraries. A blocking database call inside an async endpoint can stall the event loop. Ordinary synchronous path operations are run through a thread pool; that does not make their database driver asynchronous. CPU-intensive analysis may require a separate process or worker. Official concurrency guide. Integration and Testing Complete the SQLAlchemy lesson before adding database persistence. Use the security phase for JWT verification and per-resource authorization. Use the testing phase to cover successful requests, invalid input, missing records and unauthorized access. Override dependencies in tests to isolate external services. Small post-response background tasks can suit best-effort work. Durable jobs need persistent scheduling, retries and failure monitoring; a process crash must not silently lose business-critical work. Does async always make code faster? No. It helps concurrency during suitable waiting; CPU work and blocking libraries need separate consideration. 4. How would you structure a CRUD service? Hashing vs encryption? | Hashing | Encryption | | ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | | Designed to be one-way | Designed to be reversible with a key | | Used for password verification | Used to protect recoverable data | | No decryption operation | Decryption is possible with the appropriate key | | Example: Argon2id, bcrypt | Example: AES-GCM | Do not use ordinary fast hashes such as MD5 or SHA-256 alone for password storage. An access token is a credential presented to an API to access protected resources. Browser DevTools — A Practical Investigation For a failed form submission, inspect layers in order: 1. Elements and computed styles: Check the actual DOM, disabled controls and layout rules rather than assuming the JSX matches what is displayed. 2. Console: Read the first relevant exception and its stack; later failures may be consequences. 3. Network: Inspect method, URL, request payload, status, timing, response and preflight behavior. Separate a rejected server response from a request the browser never sent. 4. Sources: Pause at the event handler or exception, inspect values and step through the failing branch. 5. Application/storage: Inspect cookies and stored values, including expiration and scope. Do not publish tokens in screenshots or logs. 6. Performance and memory: Record a repeatable slow interaction, locate expensive work and compare after the fix. A single slow observation is not enough to establish a bottleneck. algorithms: Algorithms Definition and simple example An algorithm is a finite procedure for solving a class of problems. Its contract specifies the allowed inputs and the result or behavior it must produce. A program implements an algorithm in a particular language; different implementations may follow the same procedure. To find the smallest number, remember the first value, inspect each remaining value, and replace the remembered value whenever a smaller one appears. After each step, the remembered value is the smallest in the portion already inspected. This is the loop invariant that explains why the procedure works. An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined steps that solves a problem. To find the maximum value in an array, a straightforward algorithm is: 1. Assume the first value is the maximum. 2. Visit each remaining value. 3. Compare it with the maximum stored so far. 4. Replace the maximum whenever a larger value appears. 5. Return the stored maximum. Pattern recognition — Linear scan Interview clue: “Find the minimum, maximum, total, average, or count of values in an unsorted array.” Usually, start by considering a single linear scan. Key observation: You do not need to remember every previously examined element. You only need the smallest and largest values found so far. This pattern is also useful for finding the highest salary, lowest temperature, maximum score, or count of qualifying transactions. It is not sufficient when the interviewer asks for more structural information, such as all pairs with a particular relationship, sorted ordering, or every range maximum. Brute-force solution — Check every candidate against every value Imagine considering each element as a possible minimum or maximum. For each candidate: 1. Compare it with every other array value. 2. If nothing is smaller than the candidate, it is a minimum. 3. If nothing is larger than the candidate, it is a maximum. 4. Repeat for every candidate. This is correct but repeats many comparisons. Brute-force Java implementation Brute-force Python implementation Both programs output: Brute-force dry run The input contains five values. For each outer iteration, the inner loop runs n times. $$ n\times n=n^2 $$ There are two relational checks in each inner iteration: $$ C(n)=2n^2 $$ For n = 5 : $$ 2(5^2)=50\text{ relational checks} $$ Other work, such as updating flags, is at most proportional to the same quadratic iteration count. Therefore: - Best-case time: Θ(n²) - Average-case time: Θ(n²) - Worst-case time: Θ(n²) - Auxiliary space: O(1), because only a fixed number of variables is stored. Even if the elements are all identical, both loops still perform their full iteration counts. F. Optimized solution — Single traversal The brute-force solution repeatedly compares candidates with elements that have already been checked. For each element: - One comparison with minimum . - One comparison with maximum . - Zero or one assignment to update those values; a current value cannot be both below the minimum and above the maximum. Lesson 2 — Find the second-largest distinct element Course 2 · Original 2 · Beginner This lesson extends the previous algorithm. Instead of tracking only the largest value, we will maintain the largest and second-largest distinct values . A. Problem understanding Given an unsorted integer array, find the second-largest distinct element. Example 1: The largest value is 9 , and the second-largest distinct value is 7 . Example 2: Although there are three elements, there is only one unique value. Example 3: Sorted distinct values would be [-10, -7, -3] , so the second-largest is -7 . Our contract: Return Java null or Python None if no second distinct value exists. A null array reference in Java is treated as invalid input. This problem tests logical conditions, duplicate handling, variable updates, and how to keep track of the top two values efficiently. B. Prerequisite revision — Maintaining multiple trackers In Lesson 1, we stored one largest value. Now we store two: Consider the sequence: 4, 9, 1, 9, 7 When we read 4 , it is the only known distinct value. When we read 9 , it becomes the largest, and 4 becomes second-largest. When we read 1 , nothing changes. When we read the duplicate 9 , nothing changes. When we read 7 , it replaces 4 as second-largest. What is a sentinel? A sentinel is a special value used to represent a missing or uninitialized result. An initially unknown second-largest value should not be represented by zero, because zero might be larger than every actual array value. Java supports a nullable object reference: Python uses: Integer is Java's wrapper class for the primitive int . Unlike int , a variable of type Integer can hold null . For example: Java can automatically convert between an int and an Integer , a process called boxing and unboxing . Important: Unboxing a null Integer would cause a NullPointerException . We avoid this by checking whether the value is null first. Python integers are objects, and a variable can refer to either an integer or None . C. Pattern recognition Clues: “Second-largest,” “second-smallest,” “runner-up score,” “top two distinct values,” or “largest two numbers without sorting.” The pattern is maintaining two running best values. The critical observation is: - If a new value exceeds the largest, the previous largest becomes the second-largest. - If a value lies strictly below the largest but exceeds the second-largest, update only the second-largest. - If a value equals the largest, ignore it. This pattern is appropriate when you need a fixed, small number of extremal values. For arbitrary top-k queries, a heap or other structure may be more appropriate. We will cover that distinction when studying additional DSA patterns. D. Data structure explanation We still use only the input array and two trackers. A HashSet could store unique elements, but that would require O(d) additional space for d distinct values, plus another operation to determine ranking. A sorting-based approach could also work, but sorting the entire array is unnecessary when we only need the top two distinct values. The major Java/Python difference here is representation of the missing result: | Concept | Java | Python | | --------------- | ----------------- | ------------------ | | Largest tracker | Integer largest | largest | | Missing value | null | None | | Null check | largest == null | largest is None | | Array traversal | Enhanced for | for value in arr | | Result type | Integer | int or None | E. Brute-force solution — Two complete passes A simple correct method is: Pass 1: Find the maximum. Pass 2: Find the greatest value strictly smaller than that maximum.
