Optimized Python implementation Optimized Python — Line-by-line explanation | Code | Meaning | | ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | | def second largest(arr): | Defines the function. | | largest = None | No maximum has been seen. | | second largest value = None | No second distinct maximum has been seen. | | for current in arr: | Iterates over all array values. | | largest is None | Checks for missing initial maximum using identity. | | or current > largest | Detects a new largest value. | | second largest value = largest | Preserves the previous maximum as runner-up. | | largest = current | Updates the maximum. | | elif current < largest | Ensures the candidate is distinct from the maximum. | | second largest value is None | Detects an uninitialized runner-up. | | or current > second largest value | Detects a better runner-up. | | second largest value = current | Stores the updated runner-up. | | return second largest value | Returns the result or None . | Python's is None is the preferred way to test for the None singleton. Lesson 3 — Reverse an array using two pointers Course 3 · Original 3 · Beginner This lesson introduces one of the most important coding interview patterns: two pointers . The previous two problems required reading array elements and maintaining variables. Now we will modify an array by manipulating two indices. A. Problem understanding Given an array of integers, reverse the order of its elements. Example 1: Example 2: Important distinction: Reversing an array means changing the order of elements, not sorting them in descending order. For example: These are different operations. The interviewer may ask for either: - A reversed copy, where the original array remains unchanged. - In-place reversal , where the original array is modified using O(1) extra memory. We will implement both approaches. B. Prerequisite revision — Indices, swapping, and mutability What is swapping? Swapping means exchanging the values stored in two locations. Suppose: After swapping: Java swapping Why do we need temp ? If we write: Both variables become 20 , because the original a is overwritten before it can be assigned to b . Python swapping Python supports tuple assignment: Python evaluates the right-hand side before assigning the resulting values to the destinations, preserving the original values needed for the swap. What are two pointers? Two pointers are two variables used to keep track of positions within a data structure. For array reversal: - left starts at index 0 . - right starts at index n - 1 . - We swap their elements. - left moves right. - right moves left. Two-pointer movement The word pointer here means an index variable. Neither Java nor Python uses direct C-style memory pointers in this implementation. Java and Python mutability A Java array is mutable: A Python list is also mutable: Both now contain [9, 2, 3] . However, Python tuples and strings are immutable. We cannot directly swap their elements in place. C. Pattern recognition Look for interview phrases such as: - “Reverse in place.” - “Use constant extra space.” - “Swap the first and last elements.” - “Process the array from both ends.” - “Reverse a subarray.” These are clues for the opposite-end two-pointer pattern . The pattern is useful when the problem has a relationship between the left and right ends of a sequence. It will reappear in palindrome checking and other array problems. It is not always the best pattern. For example, a running sum generally needs only one traversal variable. A problem requiring preservation of the original array may need a new output buffer. D. Complexity calculation The loop performs n iterations, one source read and one destination write per iteration. $$ T(n)=cn+d=\Theta(n) $$ The new array stores n values. $$ M(n)=\Theta(n) $$ This is O(n) additional allocated memory relative to the original input. Under a convention that excludes the required output buffer from auxiliary space, its auxiliary space is O(1); however, total extra allocated memory is still O(n). Best, average, and worst-case times are all Θ(n) because every element is copied. This approach is not inherently a bad algorithm. It is preferable when the input must remain unchanged. We call it the baseline or brute-force solution here because it does not meet an in-place requirement. F. Optimized solution — Swap from both ends We can reverse the array without allocating another array. Algorithm: 1. Start left = 0 . 2. Start right = n - 1 . 3. While left < right , exchange arr[left] and arr[right] . 4. Increase left . 5. Decrease right . 6. Stop when the pointers meet or cross. If the array has an even number of elements, every element participates in exactly one swap. If it has an odd number of elements, the middle element stays in its original position. The number of swaps is: $$ \text{Swaps}(n)=\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor $$ Examples: | Array length | Number of swaps | | ------------ | --------------- | | 0 | 0 | | 1 | 0 | | 2 | 1 | | 5 | 2 | | 6 | 3 | | 10 | 5 | | 101 | 50 | Each swap uses a constant number of operations. The Python version stores the two indices and uses constant-sized temporary references during assignment. Therefore integer overflow is not a concern for reversing ordinary int array elements. K. Common mistakes and interview traps 1. Initializing right = arr.length . This is invalid for nonempty arrays because the last index is arr.length - 1 . 2. Moving both pointers in the same direction. For opposite-end reversal: If both indices increase, they will not converge correctly. 3. Forgetting the temporary variable in Java. Overwriting one value before saving it destroys information needed for the swap. 4. Assuming in-place and copied reversal have the same memory cost. Both require Θ(n) time, but the new-copy approach allocates Θ(n) memory while the in-place method uses Θ(1) auxiliary memory. 5. Confusing references and copies. In Python: Both variables refer to the same list. Reversing b in place also changes what you observe through a . Similarly, a Java variable assigned another array reference does not automatically create a copy of the array. 6.
